h1: Recipe kits or your own recipe for the first few brews
title: Recipe Kits or Your Own Recipe at First? | Craft Beer School
desc: Should your first few homebrews be from recipe kits or your own designs? The pros and cons of each and a sensible path from one to the other.
teaser: A recipe kit takes the guesswork out of your first brew. Your own recipe teaches you more. The trick is knowing when to switch.
standfirst: Every new brewer faces this choice. Kits are easy and reliable. Designing your own recipe is satisfying but full of traps. Here is how to decide and how to move from one to the other.
sections: What a recipe kit gives you

A recipe kit contains everything you need for one beer: extract or milled grain, hops, yeast and instructions. Someone has already balanced the recipe and measured the ingredients.

  • Reliability. The recipe is tested, so if the beer goes wrong, it is your process, not the recipe. That makes faults easier to diagnose.
  • Simplicity. You do not need to understand recipe design yet.
  • Less waste. You buy exactly what you need.

• Freshness. In India, most kits are imported or assembled from imported ingredients. Extract and hops may have spent months in warm storage. Check dates and buy from a seller that stores stock sensibly.
  • Limited choice. The range is narrower than the styles you might want to brew.
  • Cost. Kits are usually more expensive per batch than buying the same ingredients in bulk.
  • You learn less about ingredients. You follow instructions without knowing why the recipe works.

Designing your own recipe forces you to learn what each ingredient does. Why that much crystal malt? Why that hop at that time? Why that yeast? Our guide to reading a beer recipe explains how the parts fit together.

It also lets you brew with what is available. Indian homebrew shops often stock base malts, a few specialty malts, popular hop varieties and dry yeasts. Designing around those can give you fresher beer than an imported kit.
The risks of starting with your own recipe

If your very first beer is your own design and it tastes wrong, you will not know whether the recipe or the process was to blame. Common first-recipe mistakes:

  • too much specialty malt, giving a heavy, sweet or harsh beer.
  • too many hop varieties, so nothing stands out.
  • an unrealistic target, such as a strong imperial stout before you have brewed a simple pale ale.
  • no allowance for your actual efficiency, so gravity comes out low.

Our list of first homebrew mistakes covers more of these.

1. Brew one or two kits to learn the process: sanitation, temperature control, gravity readings, bottling.
  2. Rebrew a kit you liked and change one thing, perhaps a different yeast or a late hop addition.
  3. Brew a published recipe from a book or a trusted source using ingredients you buy yourself.
  4. Design a simple recipe with one base malt, one specialty malt and one or two hops. A pale ale or a SMaSH beer (single malt and single hop) is ideal.
  5. Build from there. Add complexity one ingredient at a time.

Two habits make the transition smoother. First, measure your own brewhouse efficiency on every batch, because a recipe written for 75% will come out weak if your set-up gives 65%. Second, taste each ingredient on its own where you can: chew a few grains of each malt and rub hop pellets between your fingers. You learn more from that than from any description on a packet.

Keep notes all the way. Our guide to designing a first recipe, designing your first IPA, walks through the thinking for one of the most popular styles.
A word on starting with all-grain kits

All-grain kits give you milled malt rather than extract. They are a good way to try all-grain without designing a grist. Milled malt goes stale faster than whole grain, especially in humid weather, so brew it soon after it arrives. If you are new to all-grain, an extract or partial mash kit first will make your first brew day simpler.

Cost comes into it as well. Once you have bought a few kits, add up what you paid and compare it with buying malt, hops and yeast separately for the same beer. Bulk ingredients are usually cheaper, though only if you use them before they go stale. Buying a 25 kg sack of base malt makes sense when you brew every couple of weeks, not every couple of months.

If you have never brewed, start with a kit. If you have brewed two or three kits successfully and understand your process, start designing. The goal is not to avoid kits forever. Many experienced brewers still use them for a quick, reliable batch. The goal is to understand recipes well enough to make the beer you actually want.

That understanding takes more than trial and error. A structured course that explains ingredients, recipe design and process together will save you a lot of disappointing batches.
faqs: Should my first homebrew be from a kit?
Usually yes. A tested recipe lets you focus on process. If something goes wrong you know the recipe was not the cause.
When should I start designing my own recipes?
After two or three successful kit batches, once you are confident in your sanitation, temperature control and gravity readings.
A beer made with a single malt and a single hop. It is a simple way to learn what each ingredient tastes like.
